question: Which statement best describes Server-side rendering (SSR)?
options: Because the first client render must equal the server output, any time-, randomness-, or browser-dependent logic must be deferred. The standard fix is two-pass rendering: render a stable placeholder that matches the server, then update inside useEffect, which only runs on the client after hydration. This trades one extra client render for a guaranteed match.

A mismatch occurs when the client's first render produces different markup than the server sent. Common causes are non-deterministic values (Date, Math.random), reading browser-only APIs (window, localStorage) during render, invalid HTML nesting that the browser auto-corrects, and branching render output on typeof window. React warns and may discard and re-render the affected subtree, causing flicker, wrong content, or handlers attaching to the wrong nodes.

hydrateRoot(domNode, <App/>) is the client entry for SSR: it reuses the existing server-rendered DOM and wires up listeners and state instead of recreating nodes. createRoot().render() ignores any existing markup and builds the DOM from scratch, which throws away the SSR benefit and causes a flash. The key constraint is that hydrateRoot's first render must match the server HTML exactly.

SSR runs your React tree on the server and serializes it to an HTML string that the browser can paint immediately, giving fast First Contentful Paint and crawlable markup for SEO. That HTML is inert — no event listeners, no state — until the client takes over. SSR alone solves first paint and SEO but does nothing for interactivity; that is hydration's job.

options: A per-element escape hatch for a known, unavoidable diff (like a timestamp). Use it sparingly and usually pair it with a useEffect update so the client eventually shows the correct value.

TTI is the moment the page reliably responds to input, gated by bundle download plus hydration cost on the main thread. The server HTML paints fast, but until hydration finishes for a region, its React event handlers do not exist, so clicks there do nothing. On low-end devices this visible-but-dead gap can last seconds, hurting INP and perceived quality.

renderToPipeableStream sends HTML to the browser in chunks as it is produced, so above-the-fold content paints before the whole tree is ready, and React can hydrate sections as they arrive. Combined with Suspense boundaries, a slow data-dependent section no longer blocks the rest of the page from painting and becoming interactive.

React 18 can hydrate parts of the tree independently and prioritize the region a user just interacted with, rather than hydrating top-to-bottom all at once. Islands/partial-hydration architectures take this further by shipping JS only for isolated interactive widgets while static content ships none. The result is far less main-thread work and faster TTI on heavy pages.
